edits.html:
Hypokalemia with Acidosis in a Child

Toddler with poor growth, low potassium and a normal-gap acidosis · Is the urine pH above 5.5 during the acidosis?

Source vignette Pt — 18 mo M with poor linear growth; no vomiting or diarrhea; BP 90/60 · Labs — Na 138, Cl 112, K 3.1, bicarbonate 16 mEq/L; urine pH 7.6; arterial pH 7.28 and Pco2 26 mm Hg, with normal oxygenation on room air · Q — the most likely cause of the hypokalemia; options spanned Addison disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hyperparathyroidism, juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia, pheochromocytoma, primary hyperaldosteronism, pseudohypoaldosteronism, renal artery stenosis and renal tubular acidosis
The decision point

Low potassium with a metabolic acidosis narrows the cause to diarrhea or RTA (renal tubular acidosis). The anion gap is 138 minus (112 plus 16), or 10, so the acidosis is normal gap (hyperchloremic). With no diarrhea, the loss is renal. A urine pH above 5.5 during systemic acidosis means the distal tubule cannot secrete acid. That is distal (type 1) RTA, which wastes potassium and slows growth in young children.

Low potassium with alkalosis is a different group, sorted by blood pressure. High blood pressure points to aldosterone or renin excess. Normal blood pressure points to vomiting, diuretics, or Bartter or Gitelman syndrome. High potassium with a normal-gap acidosis points to low aldosterone effect instead.

Defining criteria Normal anion gap — sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) of about 8 to 12 mEq/L; here it is 10 · Distal renal tubular acidosis — normal-gap acidosis with urine pH above 5.5, usually with low potassium · Proximal renal tubular acidosis — normal-gap acidosis with urine pH below 5.5 once bicarbonate has fallen, often with glucose, phosphate and amino acids in the urine · Type 4 renal tubular acidosis — normal-gap acidosis with high potassium from low aldosterone effect
Low potassium: sorted by potassium, acid-base and blood pressureeach of the nine NBME options sits in one row
PatternCausesWhat separates themWhy less likely here
Low potassium, normal-gap acidosis, normal blood pressureDistal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis; proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis; diarrheaUrine pH above 5.5 during acidosis is distal; proximal acidifies the urine once bicarbonate is low and often wastes glucose and phosphate; diarrhea shows in the history and gives a negative urine anion gapThe answer: no diarrhea, and urine pH 7.6 during acidosis
Low potassium, alkalosis, normal blood pressureBartter syndrome (juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia); Gitelman syndrome; vomiting; diureticsHigh bicarbonate; Bartter raises urine calcium, Gitelman lowers it; vomiting and diuretics come from the historyBicarbonate 16: this child is acidotic
Low potassium, alkalosis, high blood pressurePrimary hyperaldosteronism (renin low); renal artery stenosis (renin high); 11-beta-hydroxylase congenital adrenal hyperplasiaHypertension with alkalosis; renin separates primary aldosterone excess from renin-driven excessBlood pressure 90/60 and an acidosis
High potassium, acidosis, low or normal blood pressureAddison disease; salt-wasting (21-hydroxylase) congenital adrenal hyperplasia; type 1 pseudohypoaldosteronism; type 4 renal tubular acidosisHigh potassium, often with low sodium; aldosterone is low in Addison disease and 21-hydroxylase deficiency, high in type 1 pseudohypoaldosteronismPotassium 3.1 and sodium 138
Episodic high blood pressurePheochromocytomaParoxysms of headache, sweating and palpitations with hypertension; raised metanephrinesNormal blood pressure and no episodes
High calcium, sometimes a mild normal-gap acidosisHyperparathyroidismHigh calcium with a high parathyroid hormone levelNo calcium given, and it does not explain low potassium
Scenario bank
Management, in one line Treat distal renal tubular acidosis with oral alkali, citrate or bicarbonate, and add potassium when it stays low. Untreated acidosis slows growth in children.
Pearls Distal renal tubular acidosis raises urine calcium and lowers urine citrate, so nephrocalcinosis and kidney stones can follow; serum calcium stays normal · The urine anion gap (urine sodium plus potassium minus chloride) is positive in distal renal tubular acidosis and negative in diarrhea · Winter's formula predicts a Pco2 of 1.5 times 16 plus 8, or 32, plus or minus 2 · The measured 26 is below that range, which suggests an added respiratory alkalosis · Juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia is the kidney lesion of Bartter syndrome, which gives low potassium with alkalosis and a normal blood pressure
How NBME framed it The lead-in asked for the cause of the hypokalemia, a secondary finding, although the acid-base values decided the answer. The nine options formed a grid of potassium, acid-base status and blood pressure, and only one option fit this child.
Pairs with Part II Faltering Weight covers the first step, electrolytes with a venous blood gas when length is also low; this brief covers reading that panel. Part I Secondary Hypertension covers low potassium with alkalosis and hypertension, where renin separates primary hyperaldosteronism from renal artery stenosis. Part I Polyuria: Water or Solute covers the dilute urine that severe hypokalemia can cause. Part I Hypercalcemia Workup covers hyperparathyroidism; distal renal tubular acidosis raises urine calcium, not serum calcium. Ask: is the child acidotic or alkalotic, and is the blood pressure high?
Transferable rule Sort low potassium by acid-base status first, then by blood pressure. Low potassium with a normal-gap acidosis and no diarrhea is renal tubular acidosis, and a urine pH above 5.5 makes it distal.
Unchecked attributeAddison disease: it causes acidosis with a low-normal blood pressure; potassium would be high and sodium low.
Salient decoyCongenital adrenal hyperplasia: an adrenal disorder that affects growth; the salt-wasting form raises potassium, and the hypertensive forms cause alkalosis with high blood pressure.
True-fact-wrong-slotHyperparathyroidism: excess parathyroid hormone can cause a mild normal-gap acidosis; its hallmark is high calcium, and it does not explain low potassium.
Unchecked attributeJuxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia: this is Bartter syndrome, the closest mimic, with low potassium, normal blood pressure and poor growth in a young child; Bartter syndrome causes alkalosis, and this child is acidotic.
Class-vs-memberPheochromocytoma: an adrenal tumor on a list of hormonal causes; it causes episodic hypertension with headache and sweating, and this child is normotensive.
Unchecked attributePrimary hyperaldosteronism: the textbook cause of low potassium; it brings hypertension and alkalosis, and both are absent.
Unchecked attributePseudohypoaldosteronism: it causes a normal-gap acidosis and poor growth in infants; potassium is high in every form.
True-fact-wrong-slotRenal artery stenosis: renin excess does cause low potassium; it brings hypertension and alkalosis, and both are absent.
